newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan Semicon denies U.S. dumping charge.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan Semicon denies U.S. dumping charge.

text.p: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp on Monday denied charges that it had dumped certain types of memory chips in the United States.
"The company's products have been sold at reasonable prices around the world. The dumping charges by Micron Technology Inc are untrue," Taiwan's top chipmaker said in a statement.

The United States said on Friday an investigation of alleged dumping of static random access memory (SRAM) semiconductors imported from Korea and Taiwan would continue following a finding by the U.S. International Trade Commission.

The commission said it found reasonable indications that the U.S. industry was hurt by imports of SRAM semiconductors at what U.S. manufacturer Micron Technology had alleged were less than fair value.

Taiwan Semiconductor said the dumping charges would not have a significant impact on the company since SRAM sales accounted for less than seven percent of the firm's T$2.797 billion revenues in the first quarter.
Its SRAM sales were expected to drop to below five percent in the second quarter.
On Monday, the firm's share price fell T$2, or 2.34 percent, to T$83.50.
Taiwan's SRAM exports to the United States were US$59.29 million in 1995 and $93.46 million in 1996, official statistics showed.
The U.S. International Trade Commission finding means the U.S. Department of Commerce will continue its dumping inquiry, with a preliminary determination due by August 4.
U.S. consumption of SRAMs chip totalled US$1.2 billion in 1996, of which $357 million came from Korea and Taiwan.
Taiwan's rallying stock market fell 1.22 percent on Saturday in reaction to the allegations. The market largely ignored the issue on Monday, rising 1.78 percent to close at 8,639.37.
